title: Vary k and watch the tradeoff
description: Course activity for Exercise 3: move the k slider to refit standardized KNN regression for age at scan, from k=1 through every participant in the fitting set, and watch fitting error, validation error, and the observed-vs-predicted scatter change together.
instructions: Drag the slider, use the arrow keys, or type an exact value in the number box to change k, the number of nearest neighbours KNN averages over. Every plot and every number below updates from the actual refitted model at that k -- nothing here is a canned label.
curseOfDimensionalityNote: This activity uses the same 360 standardized cortical-thickness features as Exercise 2's canonical recipe, not the full 1440-feature brain. In many dimensions, most pairs of points end up roughly equally far apart, so "nearest neighbour" stops meaning much -- the curse of dimensionality. The Exercise 3 audit (see the notebook) found this 360-feature recipe already gives KNN a clearly positive validation score, so a smaller hand-picked bundle was not needed here; that will not be true of every feature set or every dataset.
kComplexityNote: The central tradeoff: a larger k averages more neighbours, moving predictions toward the fitting-set mean -- a simpler, smoother model with lower variance but higher bias. A smaller k follows individual fitting participants more closely -- a more flexible, more complex model with lower bias but higher variance and a greater risk of overfitting. "Lower bias" here is a general tendency of KNN, not a guarantee for every finite sample -- watch the curve and the two panels below for what actually happens in this one.
endpointNoteK1: Every fitting participant is its own nearest neighbour at distance zero, so fitting error is perfect (R² = 1) -- a trivial, not a generalising, result. Validation error is usually far worse: a single nearest neighbour is a noisy, high-variance prediction.
endpointNoteKMax: KNN averages every fitting participant for every prediction, so the model predicts the same constant -- the fitting-set mean age -- for every validation participant, no matter their brain measurements. Maximum smoothing, maximum bias, minimum variance.
trainingSampleInstructions: Training samples A, B and C are three deterministic bootstrap resamples of the same fitting pool (the validation participants never change). Switch tabs to see how much the scatter -- and the predictions behind it -- shift for the current k.
varianceProxyNote: This is an empirical training-sample sensitivity measure -- the mean, across validation participants, of the standard deviation of the three training samples' predictions for that participant -- not the formal population variance term from the bias-variance decomposition. ABIDE gives us one sample, not repeated draws from the true data-generating process, so this proxy is a lower bound on intuition, not a textbook variance.
biasProxyNote: This is an observable bias-like underfitting proxy -- the slope of the ensemble-mean prediction regressed on the observed value -- not formal bias². ABIDE does not reveal the unknown population function relating cortical structure to age, and the observed age-level outcomes still contain irreducible variation this slope cannot separate out. A slope well below 1 shows the ensemble's predictions flattening toward a constant, the visible signature of oversmoothing at large k.
reflectionPrompts: Move k from 1 up to about 20. What happens to the gap between fitting error and validation error, and why does that gap mean something different here than it did for linear regression's train/test gap?
Move k all the way to its maximum. Confirm every predicted point in the scatter plot lands on the same horizontal line. What is that line?
Find the k with the lowest validation error. Would you trust that exact k as your final reported choice? What would you need to do differently for an honest final estimate?

At a small k (say k=3), switch between training samples A, B and C. Then do the same at a large k (say k=300). At which k does the scatter plot change more between samples, and what does that tell you about variance?
Watch the binned calibration plot as k grows large. Which end of the age range gets overpredicted, and which gets underpredicted? Why does averaging over more neighbours produce exactly that pattern?
